analysis.one_liner: Bars employers and health insurers from using people's genetic information against them.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with five Republicans and five Democrats behind it, never got a hearing or a vote in any of the three committees it was sent to and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for an employer to require a genetic test or use genetic information to screen out workers, and illegal for a health insurer to deny, limit, cancel, or reprice coverage based on a person's genes. It would have required written consent before anyone's genetic information could be shared, with narrow exceptions for criminal investigations, paternity cases, and identifying bodies. It also directed a federal bioethics commission to recommend further standards for storing and using DNA samples.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who take a genetic test — or whose relatives do, since genes are shared in families — would gain control over who sees that information, and protection from losing a job or health coverage because of what their DNA shows about their possible medical future.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who takes a genetic test

how_it_helps.text: Employers could not seek, obtain, or use an employee's genetic information, or require a genetic test, to discriminate against workers or restrict their benefits, enforceable through the same remedies as the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Health insurers could not use genetic information to reject, deny, limit, cancel, refuse to renew, or raise rates on health coverage.

Genetic information could not be disclosed without a specific written authorization from the individual, and redisclosure by a second entity was covered too; exceptions were limited to criminal and death investigations, court orders, paternity, informing relatives of a deceased person, and identifying bodies.

If a life or other non-health insurer asked an applicant to take a genetic test, the applicant had to be told how the results would be used and give specific written authorization, and insurers could not use such tests to induce people to buy policies.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers would bear the cost of not being able to use genetic test results to screen applicants and price risk; life and disability insurers kept most of their ability to request genetic tests but faced new disclosure and consent requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill did not restrict genetic testing by insurers outside health insurance: life and disability insurers could still ask applicants to take a genetic test, so people could still face genetic screening in those markets, just with disclosure requirements.

The disclosure ban applied to 'entities' but the bill relied on existing enforcement machinery, and it deferred the harder questions about DNA sample storage and research standards to a future commission report rather than deciding them.

Insurers argued in this era that restricting risk assessment raises costs for policyholders overall; the bill offered no answer to how health insurers would price risk without any genetic information, a fair objection supporters would have had to address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — consent before disclosure, and bans on genetic discrimination in jobs and health coverage — address a real, growing harm as genetic testing became possible, and the health insurance carve-out for life and disability insurers was a genuine gap. The bill was a first step rather than a complete scheme, but its costs fell mainly on industries that benefited from using genetic information to screen people out.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and split among subcommittees, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, opening day of the 105th Congress, with nine cosponsors split evenly between the parties.
The House referred it to three committees — Commerce, Government Reform and Oversight, and Education and the Workforce — for the portions each controlled.
In late January it was sent down to subcommittees on Human Resources, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the two-year Congress: the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers came out ahead: no federal restriction on using genetic information in underwriting or hiring took effect, and genetic privacy law remained whatever state law provided. People taking genetic tests kept no new federal protection from discrimination during this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the 105th Congress.

for.name: 5 of 206 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Zoe Lofgren and Mel Watt

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (Chair Tom Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at the Health and Environment Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the record shows no action after the January 1997 referral.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the employment provisions
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, where no further action was taken.

sides.party_line_note: The ten sponsors were split evenly — five Republicans led by Rep. Stearns and five Democrats — so the bill's failure was not a party-line vote; it simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from using genetic information to deny, limit, cancel, or reprice health coverage. Their business model at the time relied on assessing risk to avoid covering people likely to cost more, so this protection ran directly against their underwriting interest.

Employers could no longer require genetic tests or use genetic information to screen workers or restrict benefits. The enforcement mechanism borrowed from the Civil Rights Act would have exposed them to discrimination claims.

The bill left them free to request genetic tests from applicants (only disclosure and written consent were required), but they could no longer use tests as a sales inducement. Their freedom to underwrite with genetic results was preserved while applicants gained some transparency.

Consent rules would have constrained how labs and researchers handled DNA samples, but the bill's stated purpose was to protect privacy while 'permit[ting] legitimate genetic research,' and its commission study was aimed at building durable standards the industry could operate under.
